chat.text: Remote presenters: Please, be prepared and contact the chairs to inform you are ready. Thank you.

chat.author: Steve Traugott
chat.text: Just a general comment on what I'm seeing being proposed in this session -- as someone who uses LLMs to write code all day every day, I would be more comfortable with LLM generation of DSLs and DSL compilers than with LLMs directly generating policy by translating intent.  This, due to the inherently non-deterministic and non-reproducible output of LLMs.  Use an LLM to design a DSL, write the compiler, even translate intent into that DSL.  But the actual process of generating device configs or making live changes ought to be done by the output of that deterministic compiler.

chat.author: Pedro Martinez-Julia
chat.text: Steve: In most proposals, a policy is represented in a DSL. Translating intent normally produces it and a definition of service in a formal language (also DLS, see draft-pedro-ite-02).

chat.author: Susan Hares
chat.text: How does the presentation on normalization deal with feedbavk or errors in normalization.

chat.author: Steve Traugott
chat.text: @Pedro Martinez-Julia I suspect there's an inverse relationship between DSL generality vs safety -- i.e. the less-capable a DSL is, the safer it is, easier to review, etc.  It may turn out that the top-level DSL ought to be uniquely, narrowly designed for a given organization's infrastructure.  Then there would be intermediate, more general languages lower in the stack.

chat.author: Pedro Martinez-Julia
chat.text: @Steve: Policy languages, as DSLs, are less capable than programming languages. Designing a DSL "per organization" prevents generalization. Otherwise, specializing a DSL for policies helps a lot. My remark is that DSLs are already being used in most cases. I agree with you in that those cases that do not use them, should define and use them.
